reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Advanced S Q L in Postgres
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 11, Advanced S Q L in Postgres.

Before we begin, connect this module to what you already know. You have learned how to filter and aggregate data, join tables, use subqueries, work with strings and dates, clean messy values, and reshape data. In Module 10, you also learned to protect the grain of a result. That idea remains important here.

[tts-break]

Now we will build more advanced analytical queries. We will use common table expressions to break complicated logic into clear stages. We will use recursive queries to move through hierarchies. And we will use window functions to rank rows, compare one event with an earlier or later event, calculate running totals, and create moving averages without losing the detail rows.

The goal is not to memorize difficult syntax. The goal is to understand what each stage is doing, what one row represents, and why the result is correct.

slides.title: What advanced S Q L is really doing
slides.transcript:
Advanced S Q L is mostly about controlling two things: intermediate results and row context.

A common table expression gives a useful name to one stage of a larger query. That makes a complicated query easier to read one step at a time.

A window function does something different. It lets the current row use information from related rows while still keeping the current row in the result.

For example, we can keep every employee row and place the department average salary beside each employee. Or we can keep every admission and place the previous admission date beside the current one.

That is the main idea of this module: add analytical context without losing track of the row grain.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of the module, you should be able to structure multi-step S Q L with common table expressions, trace a recursive query, choose the correct ranking function, analyze sequences with lag and the next-value function, and write explicit frames for running and moving calculations. You should also understand the difference between group by and partition by. The goal is not only to run the syntax. You should be able to explain the row meaning at every stage.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript:
We will start with ordinary common table expressions because they make complex queries easier to read. Then we will introduce recursive common table expressions for hierarchies. After that, we will study the over clause and window functions.

Ranking and sequence functions come next. Then we will make frames explicit. Finally, we will combine common table expressions and windows into useful analytical patterns.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript:
The teaching database includes several small datasets. Patients and admissions support healthcare-style analytical examples. Employees includes a manager hierarchy and salary ties.

Sales supports running totals, moving averages, ranking, and percent of total calculations. Website visits provides ordered event sequences. The variety helps you see that the S Q L patterns are general.

slides.title: The grain rule still applies
slides.transcript:
Grain remains the central safety rule. A common table expression can have a different grain from the source table. A window function usually preserves the current row grain.

A later filter can reduce the number of rows without changing what one row represents. If you cannot explain the row meaning at each stage, advanced syntax can hide mistakes instead of solving them.

slides.title: Common table expression mental model
slides.transcript:
A common table expression is a temporary named result inside one S Q L statement.

Think of it as giving a name to an intermediate step. One step might filter patients. Another step might count admissions. A later step can use that prepared result instead of repeating the same logic.

[tts-break]

The important point is that the common table expression is not a permanent table. It exists only while that statement runs.

When you see a long query, try reading it as a sequence of small named stages instead of one large block of code.

slides.title: How a common table expression is structured
slides.transcript:
A common table expression has a simple structure.

The statement begins with the word with. After that, we give the intermediate result a name. Inside the parentheses, we write the query that creates that result. The final query then uses the named result.

You can also define several common table expressions in one statement. Each one can perform a separate job.

Do not focus on punctuation when you read the code. Ask what each named stage contains and what one row represents in that stage.

slides.title: When a common table expression helps
slides.transcript:
A common table expression is useful when one stage deserves a name. It can make a multi-step query easier to read. It is especially helpful when you need to calculate a window value first and filter that result later.

Recursive queries also use the common table expression structure. Use a common table expression because it clarifies the logic, not simply because the query is long.

slides.title: When a common table expression does not help
slides.transcript:
Common table expressions are not automatically better. A short query may be clearer without one. A common table expression also does not repair unclear grain.

And it does not automatically make a query faster. Use named stages when they improve reasoning and maintainability.

slides.title: Basic common table expression example
slides.transcript:
This example creates a common table expression called older patients.

The first stage keeps patients who are older than fifty. At that point, one row still represents one patient.

The final part joins those patients to admissions and counts how many admissions each patient has.

Notice that the query becomes easier to explain because the filtering step has a name. We can first verify which patients are in the intermediate result, and then reason about the join and the count.

slides.title: How to read a common table expression
slides.transcript:
When reading a common table expression query, do not read top to bottom as one giant statement. First understand the common table expression by itself. Then ask what the final query does with that stage.

Here the common table expression filters patients. The final query joins admissions and aggregates. This staged reading style is one reason common table expressions improve clarity.

slides.title: Multiple common table expressions
slides.transcript:
A query can contain several common table expressions, and later stages can use results produced by earlier stages.

Think of this as a small pipeline. The first stage may calculate admission counts. The second stage may join those counts to patient information. The final stage may create a label such as repeat visitor or single visit.

[tts-break]

This structure is useful because every stage has one clear responsibility. When a result looks wrong, you can inspect one stage at a time instead of debugging one very large query.

slides.title: Multiple common table expression example
slides.transcript:
Run this query with several common table expressions and read it stage by stage. Admission counts has one row per patient with an admission count. Patient features joins that result to every patient and replaces missing counts with zero.

The final select statement classifies repeat versus single or none. Notice how naming intermediate results makes the logic easier to discuss.

slides.title: Common table expression with a join and aggregation
slides.transcript:
This example creates stay days in the common table expression. Each common table expression row represents one completed admission. The final query joins patients and calculates admission count and average stay per patient.

The grain changes only in the final group by. That separation makes the transformation easier to validate.

slides.title: Common table expressions and performance
slides.transcript:
Common table expressions are mainly a query-organization tool. Postgres can sometimes inline or fold a non-recursive common table expression into the surrounding query. In other situations, materialization behavior can matter.

The practical lesson for this course is simple: use common table expressions for clarity, and inspect the execution plan when performance matters. Do not assume that using a common table expression automatically makes a query faster.

slides.title: Inspect a query plan
slides.transcript:
The explain command shows how Postgres plans to execute the statement. The purpose here is not to memorize every plan node.

It is to build the habit of checking instead of guessing. On real workloads, data volume, indexes, statistics, and Postgres version all affect the plan.

slides.title: Recursive common table expressions
slides.transcript:
A recursive common table expression is used when one result leads to the next result repeatedly.

It has two main parts. The anchor term creates the starting rows. The recursive term uses the rows already found to locate the next level.

[tts-break]

A company hierarchy is a good example. We can start with the president. Then we find employees who report to the president. After that, we find employees who report to those employees. The process continues until no more matching employees are found.

Do not think of recursion as mysterious. Think of it as start here, find the next level, and repeat.

slides.title: Anchor term and recursive term
slides.transcript:
When you read a recursive query, identify the anchor term first. Ask which rows start the process.

Then identify the recursive term. Ask how the current level connects to the next level.

For an employee hierarchy, the connection is usually the manager relationship. A manager I D in one row points to an employee I D in another row.

Adding a depth value can show how far we are from the starting point. A path value can show the route through the hierarchy. These extra fields make recursion much easier to inspect.

slides.title: Employee hierarchy example
slides.transcript:
Imagine a small organization chart. The president is at level zero. Two directors report to the president, so they are at level one. Managers who report to those directors are at level two.

A recursive query can build that structure automatically from the manager relationship stored in the employee table.

The important idea is that the source table does not need one column for every level. The hierarchy is discovered by repeatedly following the parent and child relationship.

slides.title: Recursive hierarchy query
slides.transcript:
The anchor selects top-level employees with no manager. The recursive term joins employees to the current organization result when an employee's manager I D matches a current employee I D. Depth increases by one.

Path appends the employee name. Run the query and inspect how the hierarchy expands level by level.

slides.title: Trace recursion manually
slides.transcript:
A good way to understand recursion is to trace a few iterations by hand.

Start with the anchor. That is iteration zero.

Next, use those rows to find the first set of children. Then use those children to find the next level. Continue until the recursive step returns no new rows.

If a recursive query is confusing, use a tiny dataset and write down what appears at each iteration. That is often much easier than staring at the full S Q L statement.

slides.title: Recursive query safety
slides.transcript:
Recursive queries require extra care. A wrong join condition can produce too many rows. Cycles in the source hierarchy can also create problematic traversal. Test the anchor by itself.

Inspect the recursive join. Use depth or path information while developing the query. Start with a small dataset so the behavior is visible.

slides.title: Window functions
slides.transcript:
Window functions are useful when you want group context without collapsing the detail rows.

Suppose five employees work in the same department. A group by query can return one row with the department average salary. But sometimes we want all five employee rows and the department average beside every employee.

[tts-break]

That is a window-function problem.

The same idea works for ranking, previous and next events, running totals, and moving averages. The result keeps the original rows and adds analytical information around them.

slides.title: The over clause
slides.transcript:
A window calculation usually has a few pieces that answer different questions.

First, what calculation do we want? Maybe an average, a rank, or a previous value.

Second, should the rows be separated into groups? The partition by part defines those groups.

Third, what is the sequence inside each group? The order by part defines that sequence.

And for some calculations, we also define a frame. The frame says which nearby rows are included for the current row.

When a window query looks complicated, separate these questions instead of trying to read everything at once.

slides.title: Window function example
slides.transcript:
This query uses two windows over the same employee rows. Average salary with partition by department calculates the department average. Row number with partition and order assigns a sequence within each department.

No group by is used. Every employee row remains in the output, with additional context beside it.

slides.title: Partition by
slides.transcript:
Partition by divides rows into independent window groups. Without a partition, the window can operate over all rows. With department partitioning, calculations restart for each department.

With patient partitioning, sequence calculations restart for each patient. Partition changes the calculation context, not the number of output rows by itself.

slides.title: Order by inside a window
slides.transcript:
Order by inside over is part of the analytical definition. For ranking, it defines higher and lower positions. For lag and the next-value function, it defines previous and next.

For running totals, it defines the sequence of accumulation. When ordering values can tie, add a stable tie-breaker when deterministic row sequence matters.

slides.title: Window frames
slides.transcript:
A window frame defines which ordered rows participate in a calculation for the current row.

For a running total, the frame usually begins with the first row in the partition and ends with the current row.

[tts-break]

For a three-row moving average, the frame can include the current row and the two rows immediately before it.

Think of the frame as a window that moves with the current row. The size and boundaries of that window determine which values are used in the calculation.

slides.title: Ranking functions
slides.transcript:
We will compare three ranking functions: row number, rank, and dense rank.

The difference becomes important when values tie.

Row number always gives every row a unique sequence number.

[tts-break]

Rank gives tied values the same rank, but it leaves a gap after the tie.

Dense rank also gives tied values the same rank, but it does not leave a gap.

You do not choose among these functions because one is more advanced. You choose based on how ties should behave in the business question.

slides.title: Row number
slides.transcript:
Row number assigns a unique sequence even when values tie. This makes it useful for selecting exactly the top two or top three rows per group.

But if salaries tie and you only order by salary, the sequence among tied rows may not be deterministic. Add a stable tie-breaker such as employee I D when the order matters.

slides.title: Rank
slides.transcript:
Rank behaves like a competition ranking. If two employees tie for second, both receive rank two.

The next rank is four. This is useful when the numeric rank should reflect positions consumed by the tie.

slides.title: Dense rank
slides.transcript:
Dense rank also gives tied values the same rank. But it does not leave gaps.

If two employees tie for second, the next distinct salary gets rank three. This is often useful for grouping distinct ordered levels.

slides.title: Compare ranking ties
slides.transcript:
Here is a simple example. Suppose three scores are ninety, ninety, and eighty.

Row number gives the rows positions one, two, and three. It must choose a unique position for every row.

Rank gives the two ninety scores rank one. The score of eighty then receives rank three, because two positions were used by the tie.

[tts-break]

Dense rank also gives the two ninety scores rank one, but the score of eighty receives rank two.

This small example is worth remembering because it makes the difference among the three functions very clear.

slides.title: Deterministic ordering
slides.transcript:
Deterministic ordering means the same data should produce the same row sequence every time.

Suppose two employees have exactly the same salary. If row number is ordered only by salary, the database has no business rule that says which tied employee should come first.

Adding employee I D as a second ordering value gives the query a stable tie-breaker.

Be careful, though. If you add employee I D to a rank calculation, the two salary values may no longer be treated as true peers. The ordering rule must match the meaning you want.

slides.title: Ranking within groups
slides.transcript:
Partitioning makes ranking local to a group. If we partition by department, each department gets its own rank sequence.

An employee can be rank one in Analytics even if someone in Engineering has a higher salary. The comparison set is defined by the partition.

slides.title: Department ranking example
slides.transcript:
This query partitions employees by department and orders salary descending. Rank restarts at one for each department.

Run the query and notice the boundaries between departments. This is a common pattern for top earners, top products, or highest values within categories.

slides.title: Lag, looking at the previous row
slides.transcript:
The lag function is useful when the question includes words such as previous, change, or time since.

Lag looks backward in an ordered sequence and brings an earlier value onto the current row.

[tts-break]

For example, for each patient admission, we can bring the previous discharge date beside the current admission date.

The partition defines whose history we are following. The order defines what previous means. Without a meaningful partition and order, lag cannot answer the question correctly.

slides.title: Previous admission example
slides.transcript:
This admission example puts the previous discharge time beside the current admission.

First, admissions are separated by patient. Then they are ordered by time. Lag retrieves the discharge time from the previous admission for that same patient.

[tts-break]

Once both timestamps are on the current row, we can calculate the time between encounters.

The first admission for a patient has no earlier admission, so there is no previous discharge value. That missing result is expected and meaningful.

slides.title: Looking ahead to the next row
slides.transcript:
Now we look in the opposite direction.

The S Q L function spelled L E A D returns a value from a later row in the sequence. To make the spoken explanation clearer, think of it as the next-value function.

[tts-break]

If lag answers, what happened before this row, the next-value function answers, what happens after this row.

This can be useful for time until the next visit, next purchase, next website event, or next status change.

slides.title: Next website visit example
slides.transcript:
In this example, website visits are separated by user and ordered by visit time.

The next-value function, written L E A D in the code, brings the next visit timestamp onto the current row.

[tts-break]

We can then subtract the current visit time from the next visit time to measure the gap.

The final visit for each user has no later visit, so the next value is null. That is not an error. It simply means the sequence ends there.

slides.title: Sequence order must be meaningful
slides.transcript:
Sequence analysis depends on order. A timestamp usually defines the main sequence. If two events share the same timestamp, a stable event I D can break the tie.

Without a meaningful order, previous and next are undefined from an analytical perspective. Always treat the ordering clause as part of the business logic.

slides.title: Running totals
slides.transcript:
A running total grows as we move through an ordered sequence.

Imagine daily revenue of one hundred dollars, two hundred dollars, and fifty dollars. The running totals become one hundred, three hundred, and three hundred fifty.

[tts-break]

For each row, the calculation includes everything from the beginning of the sequence through the current row.

If we partition by department, each department gets its own independent running total.

slides.title: Running total example
slides.transcript:
This query first creates daily revenue for each department. Then the window calculation adds the daily values cumulatively.

Instead of reading the frame syntax aloud, focus on its meaning: begin with the first row in the department and include rows through the current day.

Run the query and watch the cumulative value grow. When the department changes, the running total starts again.

slides.title: Moving averages
slides.transcript:
A moving average is different from a running total because the calculation uses a limited number of nearby rows.

Suppose daily sales are ten, twenty, thirty, and forty. A three-row moving average for the fourth row uses twenty, thirty, and forty. The earliest value has moved outside the frame.

[tts-break]

This kind of calculation smooths short-term variation while still following the sequence over time.

slides.title: Moving average example
slides.transcript:
The query first prepares one revenue value per date. Then the window average uses the current row and up to two earlier rows.

That creates a three-row moving average.

Notice the phrase three-row. It does not automatically mean three calendar days. If some dates are missing, the three rows may cover a longer period of time.

This is why the frame definition and the row grain both matter.

slides.title: A frame based on rows
slides.transcript:
A frame based on rows counts physical rows in the ordered result.

If the frame says two preceding rows, it means up to two earlier rows. It does not mean two days, two hours, or two months.

For example, if your data has records for Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, two preceding rows can span several calendar days.

Always distinguish row distance from time distance.

slides.title: Explicit frame example
slides.transcript:
This example writes the running-total frame explicitly.

The meaning is simple: start with the first row in the ordered partition and continue through the current row.

Writing the frame explicitly makes the analytical rule visible. A future reader does not have to guess whether the default behavior was intentional.

slides.title: The last value pitfall
slides.transcript:
The last value function can be confusing because it works inside the current window frame.

Many students expect it to automatically return the final value in the entire partition. But if the current frame ends at the current row, the last value may simply be the current row's value.

[tts-break]

If you truly want the final value for the entire group, the frame must extend through the end of that partition.

The key lesson is that a window function name does not tell you the whole story. The frame is part of the calculation.

slides.title: Last value frame example
slides.transcript:
This example places two last-value calculations side by side.

The first uses the default ordered frame. The second explicitly includes the entire partition, from the beginning through the end.

Compare the two result columns carefully. The difference demonstrates why frame boundaries matter, especially for functions that ask for the first or last value in a sequence.

slides.title: Group by compared with partition by
slides.transcript:
Group by and partition by both organize rows into groups, but they produce very different outputs.

Group by usually collapses several detail rows into one summary row for each group.

[tts-break]

Partition by does not collapse the rows. It defines the context for a window calculation while keeping the detail rows.

For example, group by can give one row per patient with average stay. A window function can keep every admission and place the patient's average stay beside each admission.

slides.title: Group by stay duration
slides.transcript:
This query calculates average stay per patient using group by. The output has one row per patient.

Individual admission rows are no longer present. That is correct when the desired output grain is patient level.

slides.title: Partition by stay duration
slides.transcript:
This query keeps each completed admission. It calculates stay days for the admission and also calculates the patient's average stay using a window.

The average is repeated beside each admission for that patient. This is useful when you need to compare an individual stay with the patient's usual pattern.

slides.title: Compare output row counts
slides.transcript:
This query counts the rows produced by the group by approach and the window approach. The grouped result has one row per patient. The window result has one row per admission.

Neither is automatically better. They answer different analytical output-grain questions.

slides.title: Percent of total
slides.transcript:
Percent of total is a good example of why window functions are useful.

Suppose total sales are one thousand dollars and one sale is two hundred dollars. That sale represents twenty percent of the total.

A window calculation can place the overall total beside every sale row, so each row can calculate its own percentage without collapsing the detail records.

This pattern works for percent of company revenue, percent of department activity, or percent of patient visits within a category.

slides.title: Percent of total example
slides.transcript:
This query keeps every sale row. It also calculates the total revenue across all returned rows.

Each sale amount is then divided by that total to calculate its contribution.

The important point is that the detail row remains visible. We are adding context to the row, not replacing the detail with one grouped result.

slides.title: Top records within each group
slides.transcript:
A common analytical question is: what are the top few records inside every group?

For example, we may want the two highest-paid employees in each department.

[tts-break]

The usual pattern has two steps. First, calculate a ranking inside each department. Second, filter the ranked result in an outer query.

This is a good place for a common table expression because it gives the ranked stage a clear name before we filter it.

slides.title: Top records using row number
slides.transcript:
This version uses row number inside each department.

Salary defines the main descending order, and employee I D provides a stable tie-breaker.

The outer query keeps only row numbers one and two. Because row number always assigns unique positions, the result contains at most two employees per department.

Use this pattern when the requirement is exactly a fixed number of rows per group.

slides.title: Top records including ties
slides.transcript:
This version uses rank instead of row number.

If two employees tie for second-highest salary, both can receive rank two. Both rows will pass the filter.

That means a department can return more than two employees, even though the condition keeps the top two rank positions.

Use this behavior when ties should be included rather than broken artificially.

slides.title: Common table expression and window pipeline
slides.transcript:
Common table expressions and window functions work especially well together in a multi-stage analytical pipeline.

One stage can aggregate data to the grain we need. A second stage can add a ranking or sequence calculation without changing that grain. The final query can filter or label the prepared result.

[tts-break]

The advantage is not that the query looks more advanced. The advantage is that every stage has a clear purpose and can be checked separately.

slides.title: Pipeline example
slides.transcript:
The product totals common table expression creates one row per department and product. The ranked common table expression keeps the same grain but adds dense rank within each department. The final select statement filters to the top two rank groups.

Run the query and trace the grain through all three stages. This is a strong example of readable advanced S Q L.

slides.title: Readmission project
slides.transcript:
The readmission project combines several ideas from this module.

First, admissions are ordered within each patient. Lag brings the previous discharge time onto the current admission row.

Next, another stage calculates the gap between the previous discharge and the new admission.

[tts-break]

Finally, the query classifies whether the return occurred within thirty days.

This is a realistic example of advanced S Q L because the solution depends on grain, sequence, a window function, and staged logic working together.

slides.title: Readmission query
slides.transcript:
The first common table expression remains at admission grain and adds previous discharge. The second common table expression keeps only admissions with a previous encounter and calculates the gap. The final query joins patient names and applies the thirty day classification.

Run it and read the query stage by stage. Notice that the patient join is delayed until the final result because it is descriptive rather than needed for sequence logic.

slides.title: Project reasoning
slides.transcript:
When you review the readmission project, keep three questions visible.

First, what does one row represent at this stage?

Second, what defines the sequence of events?

[tts-break]

Third, which operations preserve the admission rows, and which operations would collapse them?

If you can answer those three questions, the query becomes much easier to explain and audit. Advanced S Q L should make reasoning more powerful, not less transparent.

slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Use this checkpoint to connect business questions with S Q L patterns. Named stages suggest common table expressions. Hierarchies suggest recursion. Group context beside detail suggests window functions.

Previous-event questions suggest lag. top records per group suggests ranking in one stage and filtering in another. The pattern choice should follow the analytical question.

slides.title: Grain checkpoint
slides.transcript:
The group by versus partition by choice is fundamentally a grain decision. If you want one row per patient, group by may be correct.

If you need every admission and the patient average beside it, a window is a better fit. Ask whether detail should be collapsed or preserved.

slides.title: Ranking checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Ranking functions should be chosen from the tie rule. If you need exactly two rows, row number is appropriate. If tied second-place employees should all be included, rank fits better.

If you want compact rank levels without gaps, use dense rank. The business meaning of ties determines the function.

slides.title: Sequence checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Sequence analysis needs two things before lag or the next-value function can make sense. First, define whose sequence you are analyzing with partition by. Second, define the event order.

Then choose lag for a previous value or the next-value function for a next value. If the order is ambiguous, the sequence result is ambiguous too.

slides.title: Applied challenge
slides.transcript:
The applied challenge asks for the two longest completed stays in each department.

Start by calculating the stay duration for each completed admission. The row grain is still one admission.

Next, rank admissions within each department, with the longest stay first. Use admission I D as a stable tie-breaker when exact durations match.

Finally, keep the first two row numbers from each department.

After the query runs, explain why the result still contains admission-level detail rather than one summary row per department.

slides.title: Module 11 takeaways
slides.transcript:
There are several habits from Module 11 that are worth carrying forward.

Use common table expressions to give names to meaningful stages. Keep the grain clear at every stage. Use window functions when you need group or sequence context without losing detail rows.

[tts-break]

Treat order by as part of the analytical definition, especially for ranking and sequence questions. Pay attention to window frames when the calculation depends on a moving range of rows.

And choose ranking functions based on how ties should behave, not simply on which function name you remember first.

slides.title: Advanced S Q L decision guide
slides.transcript:
Here is a simple decision guide.

If a complex query needs clear intermediate stages, consider common table expressions.

If the data contains a hierarchy such as employees and managers, consider a recursive common table expression.

If you need detail rows plus group context, consider a window function.

If the question says previous, think about lag. If it says next, think about the function spelled L E A D.

If you need a running or moving calculation, define a meaningful sequence and frame.

And if the true goal is one summary row per group, a regular group by query may still be the best solution.

slides.title: Next, Module 12
slides.transcript:
You now have a strong set of tools for writing complex analytical queries in a clear way.

In Module 12, we will ask a new question: what happens when useful S Q L logic needs to be reused by many reports or analysts?

[tts-break]

We will work with views and other reusable database objects. The habits from this module will continue to matter. A reusable object still needs a clear grain, understandable logic, and predictable behavior.

So as you move forward, keep the same principle: make the logic powerful, but also make it easy for another person to understand.
